clinicalPearls: Testicular lymphoma is the commonest testicular tumour in men over about 60 years and the most frequent bilateral testicular tumour
It usually presents as a painless testicular mass, sometimes with B symptoms such as fever, night sweats, or weight loss
Most cases are diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, and involvement may be a primary extranodal presentation or part of disseminated systemic lymphoma
Germ cell tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG) are characteristically normal, which helps distinguish it from germ cell tumours in the older patient
Radical inguinal orchidectomy provides tissue diagnosis and local control, after which management is systemic and led by haemato-oncology

There is a notable risk of relapse in sanctuary sites, particularly the central nervous system and the contralateral testis, prompting CNS-directed prophylaxis and consideration of contralateral scrotal radiotherapy
Staging includes CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and CNS assessment given the relapse pattern
reference.pathophysiology: Primary testicular lymphoma is a predominantly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that infiltrates the interstitium between seminiferous tubules, often with vascular invasion. The testis behaves as an immune-privileged sanctuary site, which is thought to contribute to the characteristic pattern of relapse in other sanctuary sites such as the contralateral testis and the central nervous system even after apparent local control. Disease may be confined to the testis at presentation or reflect systemic nodal or extranodal lymphoma.
additionalInvestigations: Scrotal ultrasound demonstrating diffuse or multifocal hypoechoic infiltration, sometimes bilateral
Serum AFP and beta-hCG (typically normal) to distinguish from germ cell tumour, plus LDH
Radical inguinal orchidectomy for histology and immunophenotyping
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis, often with PET, for systemic staging
Cerebrospinal fluid examination and CNS imaging given the relapse pattern
Bone marrow assessment as part of lymphoma staging
redFlags: B symptoms or rapid bilateral testicular enlargement suggesting aggressive systemic disease
Neurological symptoms indicating central nervous system involvement
Contralateral testicular enlargement suggesting sanctuary-site relapse
Extensive nodal or extranodal disease on staging
reference.prognosis: Primary testicular lymphoma tends to behave aggressively with a significant risk of relapse in the central nervous system and contralateral testis; outcomes have improved with combined immunochemotherapy plus CNS prophylaxis and contralateral radiotherapy, but late relapses mean prolonged follow-up is required.
pitfalls: Assuming a testicular mass in an older man is a germ cell tumour and overlooking lymphoma
Failing to arrange systemic and CNS staging after orchidectomy
Neglecting CNS prophylaxis and contralateral testicular protection given the relapse pattern
Attributing bilateral disease to benign inflammation
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Urinary and Male Genital Tumours
management: Perform radical inguinal orchidectomy for tissue diagnosis, immunophenotyping and local control
Treat with systemic immunochemotherapy, combining rituximab with an anthracycline-based regimen such as R-CHOP, as the mainstay for this diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, led by haemato-oncology
Give central-nervous-system-directed prophylaxis with intrathecal or high-dose methotrexate because of the propensity for CNS sanctuary relapse
Deliver prophylactic radiotherapy to the contralateral testis, another recognised sanctuary site of relapse
Complete lymphoma staging including cerebrospinal fluid examination, bone marrow assessment and PET-CT
Maintain prolonged surveillance for late relapse in the central nervous system and contralateral testis
Manage within a haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team
